opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, and I'd say it runs in both directions, but mostly I use biology as a source of inspiration rather than a blueprint. I'm not trying to build a faithful simulation of the brain. The question I keep asking is: what problems has the brain already solved that our current systems are still struggling with, and is there a principle there we can borrow?

Memory is the clearest example for me, and it's what led to HippoRAG. If you look at how standard retrieval-augmented generation works, you chunk documents, embed them, and pull back the passages most similar to the query. That works fine when the answer lives in one place. But humans are remarkably good at something these systems aren't: connecting a new cue to pieces of knowledge spread across many different experiences and integrating them on the fly. You hear one detail and suddenly a whole web of related facts lights up.

There's a long-standing theory in neuroscience, hippocampal indexing theory, that gives a nice account of this. The idea is roughly that the neocortex stores the actual content of memories, while the hippocampus maintains an index, a set of pointers and associations linking those pieces together. When you get a partial cue, the hippocampus does a kind of pattern completion and reactivates the relevant cortical representations. So we mapped that onto LLM systems: the language model plays something like the neocortex's role, processing and extracting knowledge, a knowledge graph acts as the hippocampal index, and an algorithm like Personalized PageRank does the pattern completion, spreading activation from the concepts in a query out through their associations. That gave us much better multi-hop retrieval, more efficiently than iterative retrieval methods.

The other direction is interesting too. LLMs are becoming useful as model organisms of sorts, where you can ask which behaviors emerge from scale and data alone and which seem to need extra structure. Memory is a case where, at least so far, just scaling the model doesn't give you the kind of continual, associative, long-term memory humans have. That suggests there's real architectural insight to be gained from biology.

Still, I try to be humble about it. The analogies are useful precisely because they're loose. The brain gives me hypotheses, and then the engineering and the benchmarks tell me whether they actually hold up.

r001.rationale: The response says the relationship “runs in both directions”: biology inspires LLM system design, and LLMs serve as model organisms for studying behavior and where additional structure is needed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, biology has mostly been a source of inspiration rather than a blueprint. I don't think LLMs need to look like brains to be useful, but when you're trying to figure out what's missing from these systems, the brain is the one existence proof we have of a general intelligence that works, so it's a natural place to look.

The clearest example from my own work is memory. Standard LLMs have two kinds of memory, really: whatever got baked into the weights during pretraining, and whatever fits in the context window. Neither of those is great for the thing humans do effortlessly, which is accumulate experiences over time, keep them organized, and pull up the right ones later when some new situation calls for them. Retrieval-augmented generation was supposed to fix that, but a lot of RAG is just a vector store sitting next to the model. It retrieves passages that look similar to the query, and that's it. It doesn't build any structure, and it struggles with questions that need you to connect several pieces of information that were never stored together.

That's where neuroscience got interesting for us. There's a classic theory of long-term memory in the brain, the hippocampal indexing theory, where the neocortex stores the rich content and the hippocampus acts as a kind of index that links related memories and lets you do pattern completion. You get a partial cue and the hippocampus helps you retrieve the whole associated episode, even across things you learned at different times. We essentially took that division of labor and mapped it onto an LLM system. The language model plays the role of the neocortex, extracting entities and relations from documents, and a knowledge graph plus a personalized PageRank-style retrieval step plays the role of the hippocampal index, spreading activation from the entities in a query out to related content. The result handles multi-hop questions far better than similarity search alone, and the "memories" persist and get integrated rather than just sitting in a pile.

So the relationship I'd describe is something like: biology tells you what functions matter and roughly how they might be factorized, and then you engineer whatever version of that works for the model. I'm not dogmatic about matching the mechanism. If a dumb solution works better, use the dumb solution. But I do think a lot of the obvious gaps in current LLMs, memory, continual learning, knowing what you don't know, are exactly the things brains solved a long time ago, and we'd be foolish not to at least read the literature.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology as informing LLM design, but does not say that LLM research also informs advances in biology.

astra-6.text:
I think biology is a useful source of hypotheses about how to build better systems. With LLMs, you have this very powerful component, but there are still questions about how it should interact with memory, how it should incorporate new information, and how it should retrieve the right information when it needs it. Those are also problems that biological systems have to solve.

So I’m interested in taking ideas at that functional level. What does a particular memory mechanism accomplish? Can we capture that principle in a system built around an LLM? Then we have to test whether it actually helps. The biological analogy gives us a direction to explore; it doesn’t, by itself, establish that the design is good or that the model works the way a brain does.

r001.rationale: The response says biology provides hypotheses for building better LLM-based systems, but does not say that LLM research informs advances in biology.

sol-6.1.text:
I think biology can be a source of inspiration for how we build systems around LLMs, especially when we think about memory. A language model has a tremendous amount of information in its parameters, but that’s different from being able to remember a particular experience, connect it to other experiences, and retrieve it when it becomes relevant.

So the question for me is: what can we learn from biological memory that helps us give these models more useful ways to organize and access information? You might need to retrieve something very specific, or you might need to follow associations across several pieces of information. Those are different demands, and a useful memory system should support both.

I wouldn’t assume that an LLM works the same way as a brain. I see biology as a source of hypotheses: take a principle, translate it into a computational mechanism, and then test whether it actually helps.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology as a source of inspiration for building LLM memory systems, but does not say that LLM research also informs advances in biology.
